content: The neck is the anatomical region of the body in many vertebrates that serves to separate the head from the torso or trunk. Anatomy of the Human Neck Bony Anatomy: The Cervical Spine The cervical spine, which constitutes the uppermost portion of the human vertebral column, is composed of seven vertebrae, designated as C1 through C7. These vertebrae are separated by intervertebral cartilaginous discs. The cervical spine supports the weight of the head and provides protection for the spinal cord and nerves that extend from the brain to the rest of the body. Additionally, the cervical spine is highly flexible, allowing the head to rotate, flex, and extend in multiple directions. Structurally, the cervical spine exhibits a gentle forward convex curvature, which is the least pronounced of all the spinal curves. Soft Tissue Anatomy In the midline of the neck, just below the chin, the hyoid bone can be palpated. Inferior to this lies the thyroid cartilage, commonly referred to as the Adam's apple, which is more prominent in males than in females. Below the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid cartilage can be easily felt. Between the cricoid cartilage and the suprasternal notch, the trachea and the isthmus of the thyroid gland can be identified. On the lateral aspect of the neck, the sternocleidomastoid muscle is the most prominent structure. This muscle divides the neck into the anterior and posterior triangles. The upper portion of the anterior triangle contains the submandibular gland, also known as the parotid gland, which is located beneath the posterior half of the mandible. The course of the common and external carotid arteries can be traced by drawing an imaginary line from the sternoclavicular joint to the angle of the jaw. The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) follows a path that can be approximated by a line drawn from a point midway between the angle of the jaw and the mastoid process to the midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It then traverses the posterior triangle to reach the deep surface of the trapezius muscle. The external jugular vein is often visible through the skin and runs along a line from the angle of the jaw to the midpoint of the clavicle. Adjacent to this vein are small lymphatic glands. The anterior jugular vein, which is smaller, runs approximately half an inch lateral to the midline of the neck. The clavicle, or collarbone, forms the lower boundary of the neck, while the outward slope of the neck to the shoulder is shaped by the trapezius muscle. Diagnostic Findings MRI Imaging MRI scans of the neck, as provided by RadsWiki, demonstrate normal anatomical structures of the neck. These images are useful for assessing the integrity of the cervical spine, soft tissues, and vascular structures. Neck Pain Disorders of the neck are a frequent cause of discomfort and pain. While the neck is highly functional and capable of significant movement, it is also subjected to considerable mechanical stress, making it vulnerable to various conditions.
